issues.title: Issue #774
issues.html:
Issue 774

30th October 2026

Written by Alex Ozun



Comment

I don’t normally enjoy throwing shade on other dev communities, but it’s hard not to be a little bit smug around our Android friends these days. Foldable phones have been around for 8+ years, but it took iPhone Duo, and more importantly, the Apple Developer Community, to fully open the floodgates of creativity and get the general public excited about the new experiences that foldable devices enable.

I check aggregators like beardfm.app and foldhunt.com daily, and new Duo-inspired apps just keep popping up. Granted, not all of them are great. In fact, a lot of these apps rely heavily on the hinge gimmick and arguably don’t offer much long-term value to users. But that doesn’t concern me that much. We’ve been living in bleak vibecodetown for a while now, and it’s in those gimmicks and that whimsy that I still find a spark of humanity. So keep them coming!

Speaking of gimmicks, the new MacBook Pro with a touch screen was announced on Wednesday. And I feel…a bit conflicted about it. The hero image on apple.com, with a person playing the piano on the MacBook’s screen, is outright ridiculous. But I can certainly get behind the use case of interacting with the simulator using touch input. This can be especially helpful when testing document-based apps with multi-touch workflows. And the PROLED XDR Display specs do look impressive. I really want to see it in person!

Just don’t expect me to play the piano on it 🤏

– Alex Ozun

Sponsored Link

Your coding agents need a Mac too

Claude Code can write Swift all day, but without Xcode it can’t prove the build actually passes. That’s why more teams are moving agents into a cloud development environment on Mac with Apple silicon, running the same stacks and caches as CI. This on-demand session covers how Remote Dev Environments work as shared infrastructure for developers and AI agents, where MCP fits in, and why fast builds matter even more when agents are the ones waiting on feedback. Watch it on demand.

News

Apple unveils MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display and Touch on Mac

As I already mentioned in the commentary section, Apple just announced its first MacBook with Touch. Conveniently, the announcement is accompanied by 3 new Tech Talks. I think these talks will be interesting both to developers who maintain macOS apps and want to adapt them for touch input, and to those who are looking at the new Macs as consumers and want to better understand the new touch-enabled affordances they offer: Design for touch on Mac, Bring Touch to your Mac app, Bring Live Activities to Mac

Apple forced to change app store rules in a win for roughly 15 million Australian users

Federal Court of Australia has ordered Apple to open up its devices to other app stores as it ruled that the restriction was anti-competitive.

Our Aussie editor Andyy Hope shares his thoughts: ‘Personally, I don’t think this is going to be that big of a deal in the day-to-day life of Australians, nor do I think that “Aussie App Store™” will ever take off. But I’m always open for more free market ideas.’

Design

Design the interface for functionality not familiarity

Jeff Johnson shares his thoughts on the design philosophy (or lack thereof) behind the new touch-enabled Macs. I concur with his point that touchscreens on Macs have more in common with the frustrating touch interfaces in cars than the well-motivated ones on phones and tablets.

Pocket Casts on iPhone Duo

Alex Grebenyuk, whom many readers will know as the developer behind the popular Nuke library, shares his experience adapting Pocket Casts for iPhone Duo. I really appreciate the generous number of screenshots that demonstrate the multitude of design decisions that went into the adaption process. And the Harder Than It Looks sections contains an important insight: ‘Duo also exposed a bigger gap: parts of the app needed more love on a big screen […] That will take more than one release’.

I think all the recent Day One support announcements have made us somewhat desensitised to the fact that adapting our apps isn’t always feasible in a single one-shot release.

Code

Closing Up: Why I’m making some of my projects closed-source

When Daniel Saidi writes about open-source vs closed-source development, both areas in which he’s found success, I pay attention. In this article he shares what motivated him to archive his popular open-source OnboardingKit library, and create a separate closed-source version with a commercial license. To nobody’s surprise, the decision was largely driven by the impact AI is having on open-source development. I respect Daniel’s decision, and recommend giving the article a read to get the full picture.

Business and Marketing

Don’t Launch to an Empty Room

Many developers are working on new apps right now, perhaps looking to ride the Duo hype wave, and will soon face the challenge of catching their audience’s attention. Jordan Morgan offers timely tips on how to launch your apps in an environment where everyone and their mother is shipping apps and competing for attention.

And finally...

Ok, can we please be serious and stop cracking jokes? 😅

issues.title: Issue #773
issues.html:
Issue 773

23rd October 2026

Written by Alex Ozun



Comment

Over the past few weeks, I’ve seen a massive push from developers to adapt their apps for iPhone Duo ahead of its launch date. I’ve been especially impressed by the indie dev and Build in Public communities, with many developers going well beyond what’s required for basic Duo support. There was also some interesting cross-pollination between iPad and Duo. Some developers capitalised on their recent efforts to add iPad support, extending it to Duo. Others went the opposite way and added iPad support alongside their Duo updates. But it’s not only the updates that caught my eye. There are so many interesting Duo-inspired ideas and apps floating around, like this retro-style Contacts index or this notebook app. Deck-man, the Sony Walkman app we mentioned in a recent issue, has gone proper viral, with big YouTubers featuring it in their reviews. It’s clear that skeuomorphism is making a strong comeback with Duo! Conveniently, someone built FoldHunt to capture these Duo-inspired ideas and track which existing apps have been adapted. This makes me feel like we’re back in the early days of the App Store, when we’d check in daily, eager to see what was new on the shelves. Hopefully, this feeling lasts for a while…

In fact, we might just have plenty of time to enjoy the anticipation. iPhone Duo starts shipping today, but significant supply delays mean that many developers won’t get their devices any time soon. Apple provided tech bloggers and YouTubers with review units ahead of time, which raises the question of whether a similar accommodation could be made for those developers who worked hard to provide Day One support. Perhaps Apple could allow developers to pre-order a device through their Apple Developer accounts, with some stock reserved for this purpose? I admit, I’ve no idea how the logistics of this would work, but there are many folks at Apple who are much smarter than me and could work something out. Granted, Apple is running multiple Optimize your app for iPhone Duo in-person workshops at Developer Centers around the world, where devs can get hands-on time with the devices.

Take advantage of these workshops if you can!

– Alex Ozun

News

Sean Allen shuts down his iOS Development online school

Sean Allen, a prominent iOS educator and YouTuber, announced that he’s shutting down his online school, putting some courses on sale and making others free to download. Sean explains: ‘iOS dev course sales plummeted due to AI’. I don’t know what the long-term effect of AI on online education would be, but losing the human touch that educators like Sean brought, could be devastating indeed! I hope Sean finds other ways to share his knowledge that are sustainable in this era of AI.

Code

Designing for iPhone Duo | Pockity Blog

Nikhil Nigade shares his design explorations adapting his app Pockity for iPhone Duo. This might be the first time I’ve seen someone use mesh gradients creatively to tie together a multi-screen app design. I think it’s a clever approach that also looks fantastic!

Getting your app ready for iPhone Duo: what actually broke

Most of the iPhone Duo articles I’ve seen focus on adapting iPhone-first apps. This article from Karolina Samorek stands out because it describes the experience of adapting an iPad-first app Lake (which, btw, is beautiful!). Starting with an iPad layout doesn’t automatically mean it’s iPhone Duo-ready. But it’s reassuring to see that the lift isn’t too heavy.

How to use layoutMarginsGuide in SwiftUI

I normally just skim through How-to articles unless I’m looking for something specific. But this article by Sarun I read very carefully, especially with the current push to adapt apps for iPhone Duo. Figuring out how to correctly set layout margins was one of the first things our team had to do in preparation for Duo, and believe me, it’s not as straightforward as it seems.

Tools

Explore SwiftUI Visually

Florian built exploreswiftui.com to visually showcase the native capabilities of SwiftUI ‘in its cleanest form’. It even has a dedicated page with iPhone Duo examples! Resources like this play an important role in the Apple Developer ecosystem because they fill the gaps in the official documentation (of which there are many!). Cheers, Florian!

ImageFlow | Node-based image editor

Did I ever mention that I love Mac-assed apps? 🙂 ImageFlow is a strong addition to the family of unapologetically native macOS apps. And it’s open source!

If you aren’t familiar with node-based editing, I highly recommend giving ImageFlow a try! I first learned about this concept when I tried Nuke a few years ago, and I remember thinking that it felt like visual functional programming. Great job, Daniel Fortes!

And finally...

Is your Mac ready for the cold season🧣?

issues.title: Issue #772
issues.html:
Issue 772

16th October 2026

Written by Konstantinos Nikoloutsos



Comment

Hello, iOS Dev Weekly readers 👋 It’s me Konsta.

I keep being surprised by how quickly AI is changing the way we work. This week, Anthropic shared why it replaced Git in its monorepo with Scion: source control was struggling to keep up with all the code being produced. They acknowledge earlier work like Google’s Piper, but seeing Git become the bottleneck still made me pause. I can understand familiar tools becoming less suited to the way a team now works. At the same time, duttish’s comment on Hacker News raises a fair question: how does review keep up with that pace when they still regularly find problems in Claude’s output?

On the mobile side, more stories about teams moving back to native have been catching my eye. Shopify’s move back to native caught my attention last month, and now I’ve come across Coinbase and ResortPass. A few examples don’t necessarily make a trend, but I’m interested to see where this goes.

There’s something else I can’t stop thinking about. Everyone seems excited to write new skills for agents, and the pile of AGENTS.md files, instructions, and documentation keeps growing. It brings to mind Uncle Bob’s warning that comments are future lies. I think these instructions can become future lies too. Each project’s codebase keeps evolving, and what made sense when we wrote a skill might no longer hold a few months later. So how do we get to a point where those instructions stay up to date automatically, with agents spotting what needs to change and proposing updates? Some of that context lives in the code, but some lives in conversations and meetings, where teams discuss where a project is heading and what problems they expect to face. My guess is that an agent would need to be able to listen to those discussions too, to understand when our intentions have changed. I haven’t figured out what that would look like yet, but the question keeps coming back to me.

Enjoy this week’s issue!

– Konstantinos

News

Meet Apple HomeView, a new way to enjoy entertainment and manage the home

Apple released HomeView, and not everyone is convinced?. For developers, Apple’s updated design guidance is worth a look, Widgets now covers HomeView, and Live Activities includes advice for limited-width layouts.

Personally, I suspect Apple will invest heavily in making Siri stand out over the next few years, with devices like this becoming more ways to interact with it throughout the day. I am looking forward to seeing how that develops. BUT the million-dollar question for those of us in Europe is: when will we get the full Siri experience?

And if you’re reading this aloud, I hope I haven’t just activated Siri on your iPhone. 😅

Code

Swift Actor Reentrancy: Stop Duplicate Network Requests

Actor reentrancy means that while an actor method is suspended at an await, other work can run on that actor and change its state before the method resumes. My old coworker Stavros, a staff iOS developer, recently told me that most developers he spoke to in his latest interviews weren’t aware of this problem. Give Mohit Agrawal’s article a read to understand how it happens, how it can lead to duplicate network requests, and how to prevent them.

Exploring _UILiquidLensView

Livsy Code explores _UILiquidLensView, the private UIKit view behind an interactive glass lens, looking at its resting and lifted states and how Telegram uses it. The sample menu makes those interactions easier to understand, and it’s worth a look for that alone. As the article makes clear, this is an experiment: private APIs don’t belong in production App Store code.

How I Architect SwiftUI Apps for Swift Concurrency – So the Compiler Stays Quiet

I suspect plenty of teams have reached the point where adding a single await feels like an invitation to a bunch of Sendable and actor-isolation diagnostics. It can be frustrating, especially in an existing codebase, but I’d much rather have the compiler catch a threading issue than discover it at runtime.

Karin Prater shares how she structures her SwiftUI apps to keep the compiler quiet. I recommend spending some time with her earlier articles and videos too. She has a lot of good material that helps these ideas fit together.

enumerated() Gives You an Offset, Not an Index. On a Slice Those Are Different Numbers.

Using the offset from enumerated() as an index feels like a future bug waiting for a small refactor: it works with an Array, then switching to an ArraySlice can expose the assumption. It reminds me of Juan Marin’s comment in issue 767, calling UIScreen.main.bounds “a bug waiting for a device” before discussing the iPhone Duo. It’s easy to rely on assumptions that hold until something changes. This article explains the difference and shows when to use the element directly, iterate over .indices, or pair indices and elements with zip.

Tools

Blueprint

This is the kind of tool I can imagine adding to a team’s CI/CD pipeline and having people notice straight away. Blueprint, by Mustafa Natur, turns your app icon into a blueprint-style version, with colours and badges and custom labels(thanks for that) that give testing builds and release candidates their own character. It makes them easier to tell apart and adds a little fun to the work.

It reminds me of the fastlane badge plugin, which adds a badge or overlay to your icon. What appeals to me here is the straightforward command-line workflow: install it, point it at an Icon Composer file or an app icon set, and generate a variant for your build configuration.

Article

AI-Friendly Frameworks: As Abstraction Moves Up, How Can Verification Keep Pace?

How does an agent know that the SwiftUI screen it just built actually works as intended? That’s the question that stayed with me after reading Fatbobman’s article. He explores how frameworks can give agents useful feedback, with SwiftFairy and InnoDI as examples. I’d much rather give an agent a way to check its work than keep asking it, “Are you sure?”

Pragmatic Testing for Agents

This connects nicely with the question of quality in my introduction. An agent can write plenty of passing tests, but which bugs would they actually catch? Serg Dort shares how he trimmed his Swift app’s test suite by focusing on behaviour rather than tests that repeat the implementation. What caught my attention was that the agent also deleted a test that mattered. Checking coverage exposed the gap, and he shows how he repaired it. There’s a reusable skill included, but the reasoning behind it is the part I would spend time with.

And finally...

You can now say ‘hello’, Apple-style.
